c.tagline: Ancient West Bank city built around the revered Cave of the Patriarchs and a centuries-old stone souq.

taxi.fareNote: Shared 'service' taxis run fixed routes for a set per-person fare; private taxis should have the price agreed before departure.

emergency.note: Numbers reach Palestinian Civil Police and the Palestine Red Crescent Society. Hebron is administratively split into H1 (Palestinian Authority control) and H2 (Israeli military control) under the 1997 Hebron Protocol; movement through the Old City/H2 involves Israeli military checkpoints, and visitors should check current conditions before traveling, especially around the Old City and Ibrahimi Mosque area.

hood_landmark.Old City: Cave of the Patriarchs / Ibrahimi Mosque

avoid.reason: Avoid the H2 zone around Shuhada Street and the checkpoints near the Ibrahimi Mosque during periods of unrest, when clashes can erupt with little warning.
Exercise extra care near military checkpoints and settler-Palestinian friction points in the Old City, especially on Fridays after prayers when protests are more likely.

hood_desc: The historic walled core containing the Ibrahimi Mosque/Cave of the Patriarchs, the centuries-old covered souq, and Mamluk-era stone architecture; part of this district (H2) is under Israeli military control with checkpoints and some closed streets.
A busy commercial spine south of the Old City with everyday shops, cafes, and street vendors popular with local Hebronites.
Home to Hebron's traditional glassblowing and ceramics workshops, a craft the city has practiced for centuries; visitors can watch artisans at work and buy directly from factory shops.
A residential and educational district anchored by Hebron University, with a younger, more modern feel than the Old City.
A dense commercial district around Bab al-Zawiya, one of the city's main market and transit hubs, with produce stalls, textiles, and shared-taxi stands.

water.note: Stick to bottled water; supply and quality can be inconsistent.

transit.pay: Cash (shekels) paid directly to the driver
transit.map: No official transit map; ask your hotel or locals for current shared-taxi routes
transit.note: No formal public transit system or map; shared 'service' taxis and minibuses connect Hebron to Bethlehem, Ramallah, and other West Bank towns. Access to and movement within the Old City/H2 area can be affected by Israeli military checkpoints.

bus: Shared 'service' taxis and buses connect to Bethlehem and onward to Jerusalem/Ramallah checkpoints

tip.r: Tipping is uncommon; small gratuities are appreciated at restaurants but not required.

food.desc: Hebron's own feast dish: rice, lamb and whole garlic cloves sealed in a copper pot with spices and baked slowly in a wood-fired bakery oven.

places.name: Zuwwar

places.name: Qasr al-Basha

places.name: Old City taboon bakeries

food.name: Maqluba
food.desc: Upside-down pot of rice layered with fried aubergine, cauliflower and chicken or lamb, flipped onto a tray at the table and eaten with yoghurt.

places.name: Qasr al-Basha

places.name: Zuwwar

food.name: Hummus and ful
food.desc: Warm hummus pooled with olive oil and whole chickpeas, or ful mudammas mashed with lemon and cumin, eaten for breakfast with taboon bread and raw onion.

places.name: Bab al-Zawiya breakfast shops

places.name: Ein Sarah Street eateries
places.note: The modern commercial street, easiest option outside the Old City.

food.name: Musakhan
food.desc: Taboon flatbread soaked in Palestinian olive oil and piled with sumac-stained onions, pine nuts and roast chicken; eaten with the hands.

places.name: Zuwwar
places.note: Traditional Palestinian menu with musakhan among the house dishes.

places.name: Qasr al-Basha
places.note: Roast chicken and taboon bread done in the old style, good for groups.

food.name: Knafeh and Hebron sweets
food.desc: Shredded pastry over stretchy white cheese, drenched in syrup and cut from a huge tray, sold beside baklawa, halawa and sesame barazek.

places.name: Sweet stalls in Souq al-Qasaba
places.note: Cheap slices cut to order while you walk the covered market.

places.name: Bab al-Zawiya sweet counters
places.note: Busy junction stalls selling knafeh by weight to the after-work crowd.

food.name: Hebron grapes, dibs and malban
food.desc: The hills around Hebron and Halhul are grape country; the crop is eaten fresh, boiled into dibs molasses or dried into sheets of malban with nuts.

places.note: Late-summer grape mountains, plus jars of dibs and rolls of malban year round.

places.name: Souq al-Qasaba
places.note: Old-city grocers selling dibs, dried figs and grape sweets alongside the spices.

places.name: Roadside stalls on the Halhul road
places.note: Growers selling straight from the vineyards during the August harvest.

food.name: Qahwa and shai bil na'na
food.desc: Cardamom-heavy Arabic coffee in tiny cups, or black tea stewed sweet with a fistful of mint or sage; the fixed rhythm of any Hebron conversation.

places.note: Small local coffee house where the roast smell reaches the street.

places.name: Q Candy
places.note: Modern cafe with a long list of hot and cold drinks, popular with students.

places.name: Souq al-Qasaba tea vendors

food.desc: Street coolers poured from a brass urn strapped to the vendor's back: dark sweet-sour tamarind, or bitter foaming licorice sous, both served over ice.

places.name: Souq al-Qasaba

places.name: Ein Sarah Street juice bars

landmarks: Ibrahimi Mosque / Cave of the Patriarchs (Al-Haram al-Ibrahimi)
Built by Herod over the tomb of Abraham, this monumental shrine sacred to Muslims and Jews is one of the world's oldest continuously used holy places.
Hebron Old City (UNESCO)
Vaulted Mamluk and Ottoman lanes, stone arches and a storied souq form this UNESCO-listed old town, among the best-preserved medieval urban fabrics in the Levant.
Old City Souq (Casbah Market)
Beneath ancient stone vaults, traders sell spices, textiles and famous Hebron grapes in a resilient market that has animated the casbah for centuries.
Hebron Glass and Ceramics Factories
Watch artisans hand-blow cobalt and turquoise glassware using techniques passed down since Roman times, Hebron's signature craft glowing fresh from the furnace.
Oak of Mamre and the Russian Monastery
An ancient oak revered as the spot where Abraham hosted three angels stands within the tranquil grounds of a 19th-century Russian Orthodox monastery.
Tel Rumeida (Ancient Tel Hebron)
Excavations on this olive-terraced hillside expose Bronze Age walls and Iron Age remains of biblical Hebron, one of the oldest continuously inhabited spots on earth.
Ramat al-Khalil (Ancient Mamre)
Massive Herodian enclosure walls mark this archaeological site north of the city, where tradition places Abraham's encampment and Constantine later raised a basilica.
Hirbawi Keffiyeh Factory
Palestine's last keffiyeh workshop still clatters with vintage looms weaving the iconic black-and-white checked scarf, welcoming visitors to watch and buy direct.
Sheikh Ali al-Bakka Mosque
This 13th-century Mamluk mosque with its elegant square minaret commemorates a revered local Sufi saint and punctuates the old city's western skyline.
Nabi Yunis Shrine, Halhul
A short drive north, the hilltop mosque of Halhul venerates the tomb of the prophet Jonah, offering sweeping views over Hebron's vineyard-clad hills.

train.note: There are no railways anywhere in the West Bank - the Ottoman-era branch that once ran towards Hebron has been gone for generations and nothing has replaced it. Israel Railways' nearest stations (Jerusalem-Yitzhak Navon, Beit Shemesh) sit outside the West Bank and are not a usable part of a normal journey into Hebron. Every arrival and departure is by road, so plan around buses and shared taxis rather than trains.

bus.note: Palestinian buses and shared 'servees' taxis use the stands around Bab al-Zawiya and the Hebron bus station on the north side of town. Frequent servees run to Bethlehem in about 45 minutes and on to Ramallah, and to the Arab bus station on Sultan Suleiman Street in East Jerusalem for travellers with the right documents; fares are a few shekels, paid in cash to the driver, with no advance booking and departures when the vehicle fills. No scheduled international coach serves Hebron: for Jordan you take a servees towards Jericho and then the shuttle across the Allenby/King Hussein Bridge, for which a Jordanian multi-entry visa must already be in your passport. Allow generous extra time, since checkpoints can slow or close without warning.

ferry.note: Hebron is landlocked in the southern West Bank hills, roughly 50 km from the Mediterranean and 30 km from the Dead Sea, and neither has any passenger boat service, so no ferries exist.

half.name: Bethlehem
half.blurb: Birthplace of Jesus according to Christian tradition, centered on the Church of the Nativity and its ancient grotto.

half.name: Susya
half.blurb: Archaeological site with a partly excavated ancient village and synagogue remains in the South Hebron Hills.

half.name: Bani Naim
half.blurb: Hilltop town holding the traditional Tomb of the Prophet Lot, a pilgrimage site for local visitors.
